en: The *Buddhabhāṣita-ācāravidhi-sūtra*, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master An Shigao of Parthia during the Later Han Dynasty. Thus have I heard:

At one time, the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. It was as follows: [... At that time, the Buddha was in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, at the Jeta Grove, the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada. This...
At that time, the Buddha addressed the bhikṣus, saying:

"I shall preach the Sūtra for you; its opening is excellent, its middle is excellent, and its conclusion is excellent. Its words are profound, expounding the Way that transcends the world, with the rectification of the mind as its foundation."
"Listen to my words so that they may be transmitted and practiced by future generations.
The bhikṣus joined their palms and received the instruction.
The Buddha said:
“Within the human body there are five thieves that lead people into the evil realms.
What are these five thieves?
First is form; second is feeling; third is perception; fourth is volitional formations; and fifth is consciousness. These five are what people constantly dwell upon.”
The Buddha said:
"People are constantly deceived by the eyes, deceived by the ears, deceived by the nose, deceived by the mouth, and deceived by the body."
The eye can only see and cannot hear;
the ear can only hear and cannot see;
the nose can only perceive fragrance and cannot hear.
The mouth can only perceive flavors, but cannot perceive fragrances;
the body can only perceive cold and warmth, but cannot perceive flavors.
These five [senses] all belong to the mind; the mind is their foundation.
The Buddha said:
“O bhikṣus! Those who seek the Way should rectify their minds. From ignorance one merely falls into the twelve links of dependent origination, and thus there is birth and death.”

What are the twelve? First is ignorance; second, volitional formations; third, consciousness; fourth, name-and-form; fifth, the six sense bases; sixth, contact; seventh, sensation; eighth, craving; ninth, clinging; tenth, existence; eleventh, birth; and twelfth, death.
Those who practice good will again become human; those who practice evil, upon death, enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, or animals.
The Buddha sat in contemplation and reflected: "It is because of delusion that humans undergo birth and death."

What is delusion? Originally arising from within delusion, one is now born as a human; yet the deluded mind remains unawakened and the eyes remain unclosed. One does not know where one shall go after death;

seeing the Buddha, one does not inquire; seeing the sutras, one does not read them; seeing śramaṇas, one does not serve them; one does not believe in the Way and its Virtue; seeing one’s parents, one does not show respect; one does not contemplate the suffering of the world, nor does one know the severity of the punishments and torments in the hells.
This is called delusion; because of it, there is birth and death.
One does not cease from birth and death even for the duration of a single breath; human life is no more fragile than that.
Within the human body, there are three things:
When the body dies, consciousness departs; the mind departs; and the intellect departs.
These three are constantly in pursuit of one another.
Those who practice evil enter, upon death, into the realms of hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, or spirits.

Those who practice good likewise face three outcomes that follow them: they may be reborn in the heavens, or among humans; yet those who fall into these five realms of existence do so because their minds were not upright.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “Straighten your minds;

straighten your eyes; straighten your ears; straighten your noses; straighten your mouths; straighten your bodies; straighten your intentions. Your physical bodies shall return to the earth, but your spirits shall never again enter the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, animals, or spirits.”
When one observes that people have wicked sons who are seized by the officials, it is all because their minds were not upright.

A person has a hundred "characters" (parts), just as a carriage has a hundred characters; yet most people are greedy and prone to anger, failing to contemplate the affairs within their own bodies. Upon death, they enter the hells, where their regrets will be of no further avail.
The Buddha said:

"I abandoned my kingdom and renounced the status of a Cakravartin king; having severed the roots of sorrow and birth-and-death, I desire to deliver the people of the world so that they may attain the path of Nirvana."
The one with the first degree of diligence attains the path of Arhatship;
the one with the second degree of diligence personally realizes the path of Anāgāmin;
the one with the third degree of diligence attains the path of Sakṛdāgāmin.
The fourth type of practitioner who exerts diligence attains the path of the Srotāpanna.
Although they may not be able to exert great diligence, they should uphold the five precepts:
first, not killing; second, not stealing; third, not engaging in double-tongued speech; fourth, not committing sexual misconduct; and fifth, not drinking intoxicants.
The Buddha said:
"Whether sitting or rising, a person should constantly reflect upon these four matters.
What are the four?"
First, one contemplates one's own body and contemplates the bodies of others.
Second, one contemplates one's own sensations and contemplates the sensations of others.
Third, one contemplates one's own mind and contemplates the minds of others.
Fourth, as for observing one's own phenomena and observing the phenomena of others:

if the internal mind is again disturbed, one should briefly straighten oneself and observe the body—whether it is at the extreme of satiety, the extreme of hunger, the extreme of standing, the extreme of sitting, the extreme of walking, the extreme of cold, the extreme of heat, or the extreme of lying down.

When you are about to lie down to sleep, you should startle yourself awake and sit up. If your sitting is not upright, you should stand up. If your standing is not upright, you should practice walking meditation (caṅkrama). If your mind is not upright, you should correct it yourself.
It is like a king leading his army into battle: the brave ones go to the front; once they have gone forward, even if they feel weary and wish to retreat, they do so only to reach those behind them.

Likewise, a śramaṇa who has abandoned his home, left his wife and children, and shaved off his hair and beard to become a renunciant, though he undergoes suffering for a lifetime, will ultimately attain long-term liberation.

Having attained the Way, one rejoices within oneself alone; one regards one's wife as a sister or a younger brother, and one's children as friends. Free from the heart of greedy attachment, one constantly maintains compassion and pity for all the devas and humans of the ten directions, as well as those in the hells, hungry ghosts, animals, and even the smallest crawling and flying insects. One seeks to cause them all to become wealthy, noble, peaceful, and secure, so that they may cross over to liberation and attain the path of Nirvana. Upon seeing an insect on the ground, one should feel pity with a compassionate heart, knowing that once born, one must no longer be deluded.

If one can maintain this intention, constantly mindful of serving the Buddha as one would think of one's parents, or like a prisoner condemned to death in a jail who, when a worthy person comes to plead for his release, remains wise and ever mindful of that worthy person's kindness.
"A bhikṣu who has attained the Path should always be mindful of the Buddha in this way, and mindful of the Sūtras as a person is mindful of food.
The Buddha said: "O bhikṣus!"

They shall serve one another in succession, as a younger brother serves an elder brother. Among them, those who are ignorant should consult those who possess wisdom, and they shall instruct one another in turn.
Consulting those with wisdom is like having a lamp in the darkness; do not harbor secret schemes to commit evil, and do not engage in disputes.

One should regard gold and silver as one does soil; do not falsely testify against others so that they enter into the ways of transgression; do not transmit malicious words to others or engage in mutual verbal strife; do not seek to injure the minds of others.
Do not say you have heard what you have not heard; do not say you have seen what you have not seen.
When walking, one should always keep the head lowered and gaze at the ground so that no insects are trampled to death.
One must not covet the wives of others, nor should one scrutinize the physical forms of women.
"Sitting in self-reflection and removing the mind of craving and attachment, one may then attain the Way.
The Buddha said:

"Those who seek the Way should sit in a secluded place, observing their own breathing. They should know whether the breath is short or long; when the breath does not reach the body, the body becomes exhausted. When they hold their breath and do not let it out, the body likewise becomes exhausted."
Reflecting and contemplating for oneself, who is the creator of this physical form?

One should observe the external and likewise observe the internal; through self-reflection, one finds joy that differs from that of ordinary people, and at such a time, the mind has no further need for the rare treasures of the world.

If the mind slightly wishes to follow the right path but the intention again wishes to stir slightly, one should restrain and stop it, immediately returning to its guard; thus the intention is brought back.
It is like a person who has a mirror that is not bright and does not reflect forms; by polishing away its grime, one then sees one's own reflection.
When a person has already removed greed, lust, hatred, and delusion, it is like polishing a mirror.
"Contemplate deeply that throughout the world there is nothing solid, nor is there anything permanent.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"You should maintain your minds like a square stone in a courtyard; even when rain falls, it cannot destroy it; even when the sun scorches it, it cannot dissolve it; and even when the wind blows, it cannot move it."
"Maintain the mind as if it were a stone!
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"The minds of people in the world are like flowing water; within it, there are grasses and trees that each flow away on their own, without looking back at one another. Those in front do not look back at those behind, and those behind do not look forward to those ahead. As the grasses and trees flow along, each remains as it was."
The human mind is also like this: one thought comes and one thought goes, like grass and trees that do not look back upon one another.
Having nothing more to delight in above or below heaven, dwelling as a guest between heaven and earth, one casts off the body and is never born again.

Only upon attaining the Way does one realize the teacher’s kindness; seeing the teacher, one serves him, and not seeing him, one recalls his instructions, just as a person thinks of their parents. When the mind is settled, one can achieve single-mindedness, and thus one comes to feel compassion for the people of the world and all classes of living beings, whether flying or crawling.

Sitting in meditation, one laughs to oneself, thinking: "I have now liberated myself from the world and the five realms: first, the realm of gods; second, the realm of humans; third, the realm of hungry ghosts; fourth, the realm of animals; and fifth, the realm of hell."

One who has attained arhatship can, if they wish, fly through the air and manifest transformations; they can cause water and fire to issue from their body; they can emerge from solid barriers and enter through minute apertures; and they can likewise leave behind worldly suffering and attain the path of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"The Path must be practiced; the sūtras must be read.
When the Buddha had finished speaking this sūtra, five hundred śramaṇas all attained arhatship.
All the śramaṇas rose from their seats, prostrated themselves with their heads to the ground, and paid homage to the Buddha.
This is the *Āhara-samyak-pratipatti-sūtra* spoken by the Buddha.
